{{Short description|Problem in recreational mathematics}}
[[File:FermiNeumannElephant (2010).png|thumb|Fermi–von Neumann elephant (4 complex parameters, 2010)]]
In [[recreational mathematics]], '''von Neumann's elephant''' is a problem of constructing a planar curve in the shape of an [[elephant]] from only four fixed parameters. It originated from a discussion between physicists [[John von Neumann]] and [[Enrico Fermi]], and the expression is used in physics to characterize a model with so many parameters that it is [[overfit]], will consequently match any set of experimental data, and therefore is [[unfalsifiable]] and unscientific.

==History==
In a 2004 article in the journal ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', [[Freeman Dyson]] recounts his meeting with Fermi in 1953. Fermi, while discussing a novel theory Dyson was proposing, offered the harsh critique: "There are two ways of doing calculations in theoretical physics. One way&nbsp;... is to have a clear physical picture of the process that you are calculating. The other way is to have a precise and self-consistent mathematical formalism. You have neither." Dyson countered by stating that his theory matched Fermi's own data. Fermi asked about a number of arbitrary parameters Dyson used and, upon learning that there were four of them, quoted his friend von Neumann:<ref name=dyson>{{cite journal |last=Dyson |first=Freeman |author-link=Freeman Dyson |date=January 22, 2004 |title=A meeting with Enrico Fermi |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=427 |issue=6972 |page=297 |doi=10.1038/427297a |doi-access=free |pmid=14737148 |bibcode=2004Natur.427..297D }}</ref> 
{{Quote|text=With four parameters I can fit an elephant, and with five I can make him wiggle his trunk.}}
By this he meant that the Dyson's simulations relied on too many [[free parameters]], presupposing an [[overfitting]] phenomenon. "Stunned" Dyson agreed with the argument, finished the set of articles in order for his students to get their names into the research journals, and switched to another field of study.<ref name=dyson/>

The phrase became popular enough to be used in the titles of unrelated research works, like "There is More Than One Way to Model an Elephant. Experiment-Driven Modeling of the Actin Cytoskeleton".<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Jonathon A. |last1=Ditlev |first2=Bruce J. |last2=Mayer |first3=Leslie M. |last3=Loew |pmid=23442903 |title=There is More Than One Way to Model an Elephant. Experiment-Driven Modeling of the Actin Cytoskeleton |journal=Biophysical Journal |volume=104 |issue=3 |year=2013 |pages=520–532 |doi=10.1016/j.bpj.2012.12.044 |pmc=3566448 |bibcode=2013BpJ...104..520D }}</ref>

==Construction==
Over time, solving the problem (defining four complex numbers to draw an elephantine shape) became a topic in [[recreational mathematics]]. A 1975 attempt through [[least-squares function approximation]] required dozens of terms.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wei |first=James |year=1975 |title=Least Square Fitting of an Elephant |journal=Chemtech |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=128–129}}</ref> An approximation using four parameters was found by three physicists in 2010.<ref name="mayer-khairy-howard">{{cite journal |last1=Mayer |first1=Jurgen |last2=Khairy |first2=Khaled |last3=Howard |first3=Jonathon |date=May 12, 2010 |title=Drawing an elephant with four complex parameters |journal=[[American Journal of Physics]] |volume=78 |issue=6 |pages=648–649 |doi=10.1119/1.3254017 |bibcode=2010AmJPh..78..648M | url=https://publications.mpi-cbg.de/Mayer_2010_4314.pdf}}</ref>

The construction is based on complex [[Fourier analysis]].<ref name="mayer-khairy-howard"/>

The curve found in 2010 is parameterized by
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
x(t) &= -60\cos t + 30\sin t - 8\sin 2t + 10\sin 3t, \\
y(t) &= 50\sin t + 18\sin 2t - 12\cos 3t + 14\cos 5t.
\end{align}
</math>

The four fixed parameters used are complex, with affixes {{math|''z''{{sub|1}} {{=}} 50 − 30i}}, {{math|''z''{{sub|2}} {{=}} 18 + 8i}}, {{math|''z''{{sub|3}} {{=}} 12 − 10i}}, {{math|''z''{{sub|4}} {{=}} −14 − 60i}}.
The affix point {{math|''z''{{sub|5}} {{=}} 40 + 20i}} is added to make the eye of the elephant, and this value also serves as a parameter for the movement of the "trunk".<ref>The x and y in the equation are swapped with respect to the coefficient values in the Table I of the source article to provide for a natural x/y axes arrangement.</ref><ref name="mayer-khairy-howard"/>

== Other von Neumann elephants ==
Von Neumann also used the word "elephant" as a synonym for [[Linear system|linearities]] and [[Equilibrium point (mathematics)|equilibrium points]]: elephants, equilibria, and linear systems are all equally rare in nature, thus statements about them are nontrivial and the corresponding theories meaningful. Statements and theories about non-elephants in general (non-equilibriums and non-linearities) are inevitably too broad to be of any practical use.<ref>Christopher T. May. [https://books.google.com/books?id=1D3EM0S5Md0C&pg=PA55&dq=von+neumann+elephants Nonlinear Pricing: Theory and Applications]. John Wiley & Sons, Feb 22, 1999. p. 55.</ref>
